title: Walk Time: Splash into the week's theme park news
summary:
By Robert Niles: The big news this week was Six Flags Magic Mountain's decision to retire its X2 roller coaster, which had been closed since July. The bad press about brain injury lawsuits and settlements was too much for the park, which made any attempt to smooth the notoriously rough ride not worth the effort. Assuming that any roller coaster manufacturer would take on that task.

Here is our story: Six Flags officially closes X2. Jake and I also talked about Six Flags' decision - and where Magic Mountain needs to go next - in this week's Theme Park Insider Podcast: Can Six Flags restore Magic in its Mountain?

Decisions about when to close, renovate or keep going with aging attractions inspired me to write, How can theme parks best honor and preserve their history?

In better news for the park, Six Flags Magic Mountain this week announced that it has fully energized its 4,315-vehicle solar canopy above its parking lot.

In other roller coaster news this week, Busch Gardens adds free locker time to Iron Gwazi and First test starts on Disney's new Spider-Man roller coaster.

Six Flags Great Adventure has started assembling the cars for its new Bakunawa roller coaster, which opens next year.

Elsewhere, Mattel this week released concept renderings for its first Mattel Wonder Indoor Waterpark, which the company said will open at the end of 2027 in Bellevue, Nebraska, just south of Omaha.


Images courtesy Mattel

The 100,000 square-foot, year-round waterpark will include a Barbie activity pool and FlowRider surf simulator, a Hot Wheels multi-slide tower; a lazy river decorated with Mattel Games IP including UNO, Rock 'Em Sock 'Em Robots, and Magic 8 Ball, as well as a Fisher-Price-themed water play structure. Additional Mattel Wonder Indoor Waterparks are planned for Orlando, Bradley, Illinois and Roanoke Rapids, North Carolina, with a fifth location to be announced.

title: Six Flags Magic Mountain goes full power with solar carport
summary:
By Robert Niles: Power is flowing full force now from Six Flags Magic Mountain's parking lot solar canopies.

The installation is the largest solar carport in California. It covers 4,315 parking spaces and can generate 20.8 million kilowatt-hours of electricity annually. That's enough to offset 100 percent of the annual electricity consumption of the Six Flags Magic Mountain theme park and its Six Flags Hurricane Harbor Los Angeles water park.

"This is a transformative moment for Six Flags Magic Mountain and our sustainability journey," Park President Brian Oerding said. "By investing in renewable energy, we're taking meaningful action to reduce our environmental impact while helping build a more sustainable future for our guests, team members and community. This project demonstrates what's possible when organizations commit to innovation and responsible environmental stewardship."

Heck, I would have been happy just with the shade over more than 4,000 parking spaces at Magic Mountain's formerly sun-baked lot. Generating enough clean energy to power the whole theme park is a bonus.

The 12.37-megawatt solar energy system does not take Magic Mountain off the grid. The system, developed in partnership with Solar Optimum, remains connected to Southern California Edison, with the 637,000 square-foot canopy providing power to the grid when solar production exceeds local demand and battery storage. (There's a 2-megawatt/8-megawatt-hour battery energy storage system as part of the overall system.) When the solar system is not generating enough power for the park, it can pull from the SCE grid.

Six Flags has been installing the system over the past few years, but announced this week that the system is now fully energized.

title: Busch Gardens adds free locker time to Iron Gwazi
summary:
By Robert Niles: Lockers are now free for two hours for riders on Iron Gwazi at Busch Gardens Tampa Bay.

The Florida theme park announced its new policy today, via its social media accounts. Previously, park visitors needed to pay to rent lockers for the Rocky Mountain Construction roller coaster, which does not allow loose personal items.

I don't want to give Busch Gardens and United Parks too much credit for the change, since this is reversing a policy that never should have been implemented. Let's be clear. No theme park should charge guests to use a locker on a ride with an empty-pockets policy.

Ideally, parks and ride manufacturers would design ride vehicles so that nothing will fly out of guests' pockets on-ride. Now, I know that is not the real issue on most rides with an empty-pockets policy. The real problem is guests taking stuff out of their pockets - usually a phone - as soon as their vehicle leaves the station. So parks ban those items on the ride and insist on locker use.

That's one valid approach. But with almost all parks now making in-park phone use pretty much mandatory, with tickets and reservations and even payments managed through apps, I would prefer that parks not create hassles for rule-abiding guests in an effort to control the rule-breakers.

Spend the money to staff people to monitor on-ride cameras and then kick out and trespass guests who take out phones on thrill rides where they are banned. But if parks don't wish to do that, at least make the lockers free for riders while they are in the queue and on the ride.

That also means that parks should not implement a fixed maximum amount of time for free locker use. It's not fair to limit a free locker to two hours on a ride when its wait time pushes that limit. Other parks have figured out how to extend free locker time when a ride's wait time grows or there's a downtime without a queue dump. All parks should do the same.

So, credit to Busch Gardens for taking one step toward doing the right thing. That's better than not taking that step, I guess. All other theme parks now charging guests to rent lockers on rides with empty-pockets policies need to change that policy, as well.

Back-door upcharges for what should be included with park admission need to stop.

title: Universal looks to improve show, via new patent applications
summary:
By Robert Niles: We have three new patent applications from Universal this week, including proposals for more realistic show animations, more responsive interactive gameplay, and easier-to-find lockers.

First, the show animation. In "Show Effect System for Attraction System," Universal details its plans to address the problem of one physical thing moving another in a show scene. Think of an animated character pushing buttons, moving boxes or pulling levers - that sort of thing. Now, if the character actually was contacting those props, that would cause wear over time, raising maintenance costs.

And if the character was not actually contacting that prop, well, that would look fake and unconvincing. So how can a character actually contact and "move" a prop without causing wear? Universal's patent application addresses that, by describing a linkage system between the character and the prop, with an actuator doing the moving. You can read the details here: Show Effect System for Attraction System.

In "Interactive Systems and Methods With Feedback Devices," Universal describes its proposal for connecting RFID tags and microcontrollers so that guests can get some form of visual or physical feedback when using RFID-enabled interactive devices in the park. Think of the Second Generation Interactive Wands in The Wizarding World of Harry Potter lands at Universal Orland, which are designed to provide haptic and visual feedback when you cast a spell successfully. However, what Universal describes here could enable far more engagement than that. The patent application details the process by which users' device and targets communicate with one another to trigger animation and feedback. You can see the full description here: Interactive Systems and Methods With Feedback Devices.

Finally, Universal's third patent application this week addresses the locker systems that parks use for certain thrill rides. One of the problems with these massive locker banks is finding the specific locker where you stashed your stuff. In "Locker Management Systems and Methods," Universal proposes a "locker guidance module" that activates a lighting system to direct a guest to their specific locker.

Let's say you get off a ride and scan your ticket to reopen your locker. Universal's system also would use lightning to direct your attention toward that locker, so that you can spot it more easily. Here's how they do it: Locker Management Systems and Methods.

title: Let�s de-influence a Walt Disney World vacation
summary:
By Robert Niles: Thinking about a trip to Walt Disney World? Overwhelmed by all the TikToks, Instagrams and YouTube videos from influencers telling you all the stuff that you �absolutely must do!� when going to Disney?

I�m here to reassure you that you can ignore all that. Let�s de-influence a Walt Disney World visit and get down to just the information you really need to know.

When to visit� and when not

The Walt Disney World Resort is open every day of the year. But the weather in Central Florida can be unbearably hot and humid for many visitors during the summer. Unfortunately, that�s vacation season for most families with school-aged children. As a result, the spring break and winter holiday weeks have become the new �high season� at Disney in Florida.

Disney�s also packed during weekends when the resort stages its runDisney marathons and half-marathons. You will want to avoid these weeks in 2027, if you no one in your family is participating:

  • January 6-10
  • February 25-March 1
  • April 8-11

Before you decide when to visit, read through the rest of the information below, because that might influence your options for dates and where to stay � decisions that you will need to make before you price your best choice.

Where to stay

If you stay at one of Walt Disney World�s 32 on-site resort hotels, or one of 15 other non-Disney hotels within the resort area, you will get 30 minutes of early entry into Disney�s theme parks on every day for which you have a park ticket. That gives you a 30-minute head start before the park opens to regular guests to go on rides that will have long mid-day waits.

Staying on-site with Disney also allows you a head start in booking dining reservations as well as buying Disney�s line-reducing Lightning Lane passes. More on that in a bit.

Staying on site does not mean that you will be staying within walking distance of the parks. Most on-site Disney hotel guests will get to the parks riding crowded resort buses, though monorails, boats and aerial tramways will be available at select resorts, going to the nearest park or two. Off-site guests will need to drive and park at one of the parks, for $35 a day. If you are staying at a Disney hotel, theme park parking is free.

If you book a vacation with Disney for one of its hotels, you also might have the option of buying a Disney Dining Plan that includes free food for children ages 3-9. That�s one of many promotions that Disney will offer from time to time to entice people to visit. Talk to a travel agent or check Disney�s website if you are interested in those. In general, Disney does not offer deep discounts, so don�t go in expecting to find them.

If none of that matters to you, then go ahead and find the best deal that you can for one of the many off-site hotels near Disney in the Orlando area. Every major chain has hotels here, so a lot of loyalty points might help you book a free or reduced-price room.

So what�s a Lightning Lane and why does it matter?

Most Disney theme park attractions have two queues for people waiting to ride: a standby queue and a Lightning Lane.

The standby queue is free with park admission. The Lightning Lane costs extra. The benefit is that the wait time in the Lightning Lane should be substantially shorter than the standby queue.

If you are willing to pay for Lightning Lane for everyone in your family, when you visit and when you get up and head into the parks for the day might not matter as much as if you want to use only standby queues. If you are using only standby, you will want to visit at less-crowded times to help keep you from spending many hours each day waiting instead of riding.

So how much is Lightning Lane? Disney sells this perk in three ways:

  • Lightning Lane Premier Pass: One-time access to each Lightning Lane in an individual park for one day, whenever you want, priced from about $130 to more than $400 per person.
  • Lightning Lane Single Pass: One-time access to one Lightning Lane attraction, priced from around $11-24, depending upon the specific ride.
  • Lightning Lane Multi Pass: One-time access to Lightning Lane attractions that do not offer Single Pass, on a scheduled basis. The price varies by park and by date, ranging from around $16 to $40. This one can be complicated for Disney beginners, but I explain it all here: How to use Lightning Lane at Walt Disney World.

If you stay on-site with Disney, you can buy Lightning Lane passes up to seven days in advance of your arrival. You then can buy Lightning Lanes for the length of your stay, up to 14 days. Other guests can buy Lightning Lanes only three days in advance. You can book your first three Lightning Lane attraction times when you buy your Lightning Lane pass, so staying on site gives you a head start on claiming early ride times for the most popular rides at the resort.

If you are interested in Lightning Lane, you should buy your pass and start reserving ride times as soon as you are allowed. Then get familiar with maximizing the value of your purchase by reading our guide, How to use Lightning Lane at Walt Disney World.

So what should you ride?

Whatever you want. Read our one-page visitors guides to each Walt Disney World theme park to see what is available at each park, maybe watch some on-ride videos, and to find out which rides have the longest mid-day wait times:

  • Magic Kingdom
  • EPCOT
  • Disney�s Hollywood Studios
  • Disney�s Animal Kingdom

Nothing at Disney is a �must do,� unless you want it to be. Plenty of families love experiences in the park that you might never see hyped up on TikTok.

If you are considering Disney�s Park Hopper ticket option, note that Walt Disney World�s theme parks are located miles away from each other and travel time between the parks can take up to an hour at times. The decision is up to you, but I recommend that first-time visitors avoid Park Hopping and opt for the simpler, and cheaper, approach of visiting just one park per day.

Dining reservations

Obviously, you will need to eat when visiting the parks. It�s easy for fans to get caught up in a complicated process for reserving dining times at Disney�s table-service restaurants.

Dining reservations can be made via the Disney World website or a travel agent, and each date's reservations open 60 days in advance, at about 5:45am Eastern Time. Disney's on-site hotel guests may make reservations for their entire stay (up to 10 days) starting 60 days before their check-in date. That gives Disney's on-site hotel guests an advantage in making reservations for the most popular restaurants.

Or you can just book what is available on the day of your visit, via the official Walt Disney World app, which you really should download in advance of your visit. The food at Disney is not as special as the rides and shows there are, so make getting on the attractions that catch your eye your priority.

That said, character meals can be a nice way to meet and take photos with select Disney characters while also sitting down and enjoying a meal. Yet that�s also why those reservations can be the toughest to get. Try to book as soon as reservations for your date open. But if you don�t get it, don�t sweat.

You do not need to pay some third party to make a reservation for you. Again, nothing is a �must do.� You will find plenty of food options in the park, including walk-up restaurants where you might even be able to use mobile ordering via Disney�s app. And snack stands abound, especially at EPCOT during the Food & Wine, Flower & Garden, Festival of Arts, and Festival of Holidays celebrations, which happen for almost all of the year.

The dominant flavors at Disney are salt and sugar. If you don�t get caught up in how Disney has chosen to style that salt and sugar, then you can ignore the influencers and their Instagram posts. Go for what looks good to you in the app, but don�t waste ride time to get one choice over another.

Pace yourself

Finally, with Walt Disney World�s theme parks being so far from another � and the hotels � you�re likely not going to want to spend the time to go back and forth during the day. So plan to pace yourself when visiting. Be realistic about what you and your family can handle. Especially if no one is in the habit of walking 10,000 to 20,000 steps a day, or more.

If someone in your family has a disability and will need an accommodation when visiting Disney, the resort has a page that details those.

That�s it. That�s what you really need to know to before visiting Walt Disney World. Now you are ready to buy your tickets and book your trip, which you can do on Disney�s website or through a travel agent. If you have more questions, the readers at Theme Park Insider always are happy help over on our Discussion Forum, too.

title: How can theme parks best honor and preserve their history?
summary:
By Robert Niles: Six Flags Magic Mountain did the right thing by retiring X2.

As I wrote in my Orange County Register column today, theme parks need to be more aggressive about closing rough and painful thrill rides, especially when those rides develop a history of injuring guests with no pre-existing medical conditions.

But I don't want to talk about safety now - we have covered that topic extensively here on Theme Park Insider. Today, I want to talk about history, instead.

X2 was an important roller coaster in amusement park history. It deserves to be remembered for the technical innovation that it brought to the coaster industry, and it also deserves to be remembered for the problems that it had.

Part of the purpose in remembering, teaching, and preserving history is so that we will not forget the lessons that history should be teaching us. X2 and its predecessor X combined several elements that have become popular in modern roller coasters, including a face-down 90-degree dive drop, wing-mounted coaster seats, and programmed seat rotation.

X2's legacy lives on whenever a guest boards a coaster that has improved upon those elements and walks away a fan. A generation of coaster designers have learned from what X and X2 taught, by creating these new thrill machines and others yet to come. The lessons of X2 have been learned, and now it is up to those new coasters to leave their own legacies and teach their own lessons. No one needs to see the skeleton of X2 looming over Magic Mountain to remember what the coaster did and what it meant to the industry and its fans.

The opening of Disneyland in 1955 created the modern era of theme parks. But as Disneyland and the parks that followed it approach and pass the age of the average American lifespan, the question of what parks should do to preserve their history will resonate with more and more fans.

Rides that continue to resonate with fans, driving ticket and pass sales, will continue to get the investment that they need to remain in operation. Great coasters inevitably become a Ship of Theseus, with their tracks, trains, control systems, and stations replaced over time. The controversy comes when an attraction holds historical significance but is sliding into contemporary irrelevance.

Many parks are choosing to honor these rides' legacies by reimagining them. This was pretty much Rocky Mountain Construction's original business plan - rebuilding aging, historic wooden coasters to appeal to a new generation of riders. Even shows sometimes call back to their predecessors. Just look at what Busch Gardens Williamsburg has planned for its upcoming Return to Corkscrew Hill for an example.

I love the respect that parks show longtime fans by acknowledging and honoring its attractions' history in these ways. Smart managers understand that a park's history can be a living attraction itself. They find ways to connect that history to the experience that a critical mass of customers want today.

One of the quickest ways to destroy a business is by chasing new customers while ignoring - or worse, disrespecting - those who have been with you for years. That's why I was happy to read Six Flags Magic Mountain President Brian Oerding acknowledge X2's history and the love that many fans had for it when announcing the ride's retirement this morning.

But keeping a painful coaster with what had become a terrible public reputation was not the way to honor that fan devotion. The best way that Six Flags Magic Mountain can honor the legacy of X2 is to install another amazing, jaw-dropping, innovative coaster that gets fans talking and making plans to visit the park.

I like what I have seen from Magic Mountain's plans for its new Thrill Glider next year. But as a Southern Californian, I want to see Magic Mountain bringing the best of the roller coaster world to the Los Angeles area. Maybe that's America's first installation of a Mack Rides Stryker coaster. Or a great new track design for an Intamin LSM Launch coaster or a Mack Rides Xtreme Spinning Coaster. A world-class, story-driven family coaster would provide a nice addition to the park's current coaster line-up, too.

When older fans express nostalgia for the favorite parks, it's not necessarily because we want to go back on those same old rides and see those same old shows again. It's because we want to feel again the way that those rides and shows once made us feel.

Creating new experiences that honor and pay off the expectations of the past is the best way that parks can hold on to their current fans while appealing to new ones. Cutting ties with a troubled coaster that was holding back the park was a smart move by Six Flags Magic Mountain. I would love to see the park follow that with an equally impressive next step toward developing a new attraction that will get fans across the region and around the world as excited as X and X2 once did.

title: Six Flags officially closes X2
summary:
By Robert Niles: Well, that's it.

Six Flags has thrown in the towel and given up on X2. Six Flags Magic Mountain President Brian Oerding made it official this morning.

"While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it�s the right thing to do," he wrote on Six Flags' website. "Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously."

X2 has been closed since July, following a reported injury accident. The ride has been named in several lawsuits and news stories as a result of injuries reported by riders.

X2 opened in 2008 as a reimagining of X, the Arrow 4-D coaster that opened in 2002. The original X pretty much sunk Arrow Dynamics (see X's Failure Threatens Many in Theme Park Industry). S & S worked with Six Flags on the X2 return, but as the coaster has aged, complaints have mounted about rough rides on the wing-style rotating seats, especially around its raven turn.

With X2's closure, Magic Mountain now has 16 operating roller coasters. The park once held the world record for most coasters, but now trails Energylandia, Canada's Wonderland, Cedar Point and Wonderland Eurasia in T�rkiye.
